newsitem.title: USA: Carriers still struggle to overcome Valujet crash.
newsitem.headline: Carriers still struggle to overcome Valujet crash.

text.p: It has been a year since the ValuJet Inc crash in Florida's Everglades, but the low-cost airline industry is just beginning to overcome safety concerns from the tragedy last May 11, analysts said.

"(Denver-based) Frontier (Airlines Inc) was the only U.S. low cost airline that wasn't hit dramatically by the ValuJet fallout, and this was because the public thought, incorrectly, that they had been around for years," said Russell Winter, an airline industry analyst at Hambrecht & Quist in San Francisco.

Known for its fast growth, older aircraft and a string of incidents including a hard landing in Nashville and overrunning a Washington runway early last year, Atlanta-based ValuJet flew into a nightmare on a sunny Saturday afternoon a year ago this weekend.

That day, fire broke out on Atlanta-bound Flight 592 shortly after takeoff from Miami International Airport, a disaster linked to old oxygen canisters that had been incorrectly loaded into the jet's cargo hold.
The jet's pilot radioed for help and attempted to turn back, but the aircraft plunged earthward, with all 110 people on board believed dead before impact.

Afterward, reports of the devastation at the watery crash site, coupled with investigators' questions about ValuJet's safety procedures and its eventual grounding, cast a cloud on the entire discount air travel industry.
Potential customers feared that newer, lesser-known carriers were cutting costs by scrimping on safety.

For example, AirTran Airways, which has about 4.2 percent of the important Orlando, Fla., market and serves 21 cities with 10 Boeing 737-200s, said reservations dropped 23 percent the week following the ValuJet crash.

ValuJet lost $41.5 million in 1996, including a $68 million charge taken to reflect its grounding in the wake of the crash. Privately held Kiwi International Air Lines Inc filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy last fall.

Another privately held carrier, Carnival Air Lines, which agreed to be acquired by the much smaller Pan American World Airways in March, said it had been consistently profitable until the ValuJet crash but had been in the red ever since. Analysts said the deal gave Carnival the chance to link itself to a well-known airline brand name.

"The no-frills airlines face a real issue which is that they can't be seen as no-frills in terms of safety. If you're new, the public seems to be very wary about the few dollars you are saving," said Peter Harleman, a managing director at the brand identity consultancy Landor Associates.
"Pan Am's a great name. If they can deliver on it in terms of acceptable service, they have a special platform there," he said.

But analysts said they expected the stronger startup carriers would turn around, if their finances were sound and they had found niche markets where they were not overly vulnerable to predatory pricing from more established carriers. "Just as the majors recovered impressively from safety fears due to terrorism in 1991, the startups, as they are still described, are now similarly recovering from safety fears due to ValuJet in 1996," Winter said.

Michael Boyd, president of Aviation Systems Research in Golden, Colo., an aviation consulting and research firm, said many of the small carriers that have had financial problems since the ValuJet crash had problems long before May 11, 1996, largely because they had failed to attract significant customer bases.
"A lot of them didn't start with a huge customer base to begin with. It (the ValuJet crash) may have enhanced a situation that was already in place," he said.

Similarly, he said, those with solid strategies would survive for the long term, with ValuJet-linked problems only a blip. "Right now, there are only two or three that are really out of the woods and are really strong -- AirTran in Orlando and Frontier in Denver," he said. "The thing to watch out for is airlines that have hallucinations of grandeur. A startup who comes along and says 'We are going to be a substantial player in this city or that city,' -- the chances of that happening are nil."
